whenAndWhere: September 1992, in eleven specialist shops. A Detroit with no radio for this music, a Berlin still filling the empty buildings of the east, a Rotterdam that has just invented a harder version of it, and a London counting the cost of the summer's free festivals.
inTheAir: The majors are cutting vinyl in favour of the compact disc, so a twelve-inch is becoming a refusal rather than the default format.
Detroit producers are watching European labels sell their own records back to them, and unpaid licensing is the standing subject of every conversation.
Rostock burned in August with a crowd standing by applauding, and nothing shipped into Germany this month arrives outside that.
The DJ is now billed above the record, and magazines want a photograph and a first name before they will write anything at all.
contested: Some say anonymity protects the music from the star system; others answer that a black music from Detroit with its authors erased is exactly how it gets taken.
Some say five hundred and no repress keeps it out of the wrong hands; others answer that it only means Italian bootleggers press it and keep the money.
exhausted: The smiley, dead since 1990 and still on half the flyers in the shop.
Fractals and Mandelbrot swirls, four years of the same screensaver.
Chrome lettering with a lens flare, house style of every hardcore night.
Cartoon aliens and borrowed cartoon characters over a bill of fifteen names.

whoIsWatching.audience: A man of twenty-three stands in a listening booth on a Saturday spending rent money. He already owns four records that sound like this one and can tell inside eight bars when he is being sold something. What holds him is a fact he cannot look up anywhere. What loses him is anything that reads like a press release.
whoIsWatching.adversary: A licensing scout at a large label who would pay well for a name and a photograph, and who, refused, will have it repressed unlicensed in Italy within six weeks.

stakesLevelWhy: Five hundred copies and no second pressing makes it unrepeatable, but what is at stake is whether a record is read correctly, not what happens to anyone.
